Unit 9 e-Portfolio Activity – CNN Object Recognition (CIFAR-10)¶

Task: read Wall (2019) and record thoughts on the ethical and social implications of this CNN technology (see the separate reflection draft). Run the CNN notebook, review its sections, and change the test image used for prediction (x_test[16]) to other values (1–15) to see whether the model predicts correctly.

This completed copy runs the original notebook first; the original file is unchanged. Changes needed to run it:

  • Data: CIFAR-10 is loaded from the copy saved in the Unit 11 project (cifar10.npz) instead of being downloaded. Its test set is identical to the official dataset, so the single-image exercise is unaffected. Its training images are in a different order, so the first training image is not the frog in the original, and the validation split (the first 10,000 training images) contains different images.
  • model.predict_classes() no longer exists in Keras 3; it is replaced with np.argmax(model.predict(...)).
  • Training prints one line per epoch (verbose=2) instead of a progress bar.

Get the Dataset¶

CIFAR-10 is an established computer-vision dataset used for object recognition. It is a subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset and consists of 60,000 32x32 color images containing one of 10 object classes, with 6000 images per class. It was collected by Alex Krizhevsky, Vinod Nair, and Geoffrey Hinton. The dataset is popularly used to train image classification models

In [4]:

npz_path = next(p for base in [Path('.'), Path('..')] for p in sorted(base.glob('**/cifar10.npz')))
data = np.load(npz_path)
x_train_all, y_train_all = data['x_train'], data['y_train'].reshape(-1, 1)   # same shapes as cifar10.load_data()
x_test, y_test = data['x_test'], data['y_test'].reshape(-1, 1)
print('Loaded', npz_path)

Creating the Validation dataset¶

For small data we usually go with: * 60% for Training * 20% Validation * 20% Testing

Only the final selected model gets to see the testing data. This helps us to ensure that we have close to real data in real-world when the model is deployed. Only our best model gets to see our testing dataset. Because it will give us a realistic impression of how our model will do in the real world

However, if the dataset is enormous.: * 1% for is used for validation * 1% for is used for testing

NOTE:¶

* FILTERS: Typical values for the number of filters can be determined by the data set's complexity. So essentially the larger the images, the more variety and the more classes you're trying to classify then the more filters you should have.

* Most times people typically pick filter based on powers of 2, for example, 32. However, if you have more complex data like road signs etc. you should be starting with a higher filter value

The default STRIDE value is 1 x 1 pixel

BUILDING THE MODEL¶

In [29]:
model = Sequential()

## ************* FIRST SET OF LAYERS *************************

# CONVOLUTIONAL LAYER
model.add(Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=(4,4),input_shape=(32, 32, 3), activation='relu',))
# POOLING LAYER
model.add(MaxPool2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

## *************** SECOND SET OF LAYERS ***********************
#Since the shape of the data is 32 x 32 x 3 =3072 ... 
#We need to deal with this more complex structure by adding yet another convolutional layer

# *************CONVOLUTIONAL LAYER
model.add(Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=(4,4),input_shape=(32, 32, 3), activation='relu',))
# POOLING LAYER
model.add(MaxPool2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

# FLATTEN IMAGES FROM 32 x 32 x 3 =3072 BEFORE FINAL LAYER
model.add(Flatten())

# 256 NEURONS IN DENSE HIDDEN LAYER (YOU CAN CHANGE THIS NUMBER OF NEURONS)
model.add(Dense(256, activation='relu'))

# LAST LAYER IS THE CLASSIFIER, THUS 10 POSSIBLE CLASSES
model.add(Dense(10, activation='softmax'))


model.compile(loss='categorical_crossentropy',
              optimizer='adam',
              metrics=['accuracy'])

3. Is the model confident when it is wrong?¶


















In [51]:






test_probs = model.predict(x_test, verbose=0)
confidence = test_probs.max(axis=1)
correct = predictions == y_test.ravel()
print(f"Average confidence when correct: {confidence[correct].mean():.1%}")
print(f"Average confidence when wrong:   {confidence[~correct].mean():.1%}")
print(f"Wrong predictions made with over 90% confidence: {(confidence[~correct] > 0.9).sum()} "
      f"({(confidence[~correct] > 0.9).mean():.1%} of all mistakes)")

4. How robust is the model to small, harmless changes?¶
Each test image is changed in a way that does not change what a person sees: mirrored left–right, made 30% darker,
or given a little random noise. The question is how often the prediction changes.


















In [52]:






rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
variants = {
    "original": x_test,
    "mirrored left-right": x_test[:, :, ::-1, :],
    "30% darker": x_test * 0.7,
    "slight noise (sd 0.05)": np.clip(x_test + rng.normal(0, 0.05, x_test.shape), 0, 1),
}
rows = []
for name, xv in variants.items():
    pv = np.argmax(model.predict(xv, verbose=0), axis=-1)
    rows.append({"test images": name, "accuracy": (pv == y_test.ravel()).mean(),
                 "predictions changed vs original": (pv != predictions).mean()})
robust = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("test images")
(robust * 100).round(1).astype(str) + " %"

Findings¶
How the notebook works. CIFAR-10 has 60,000 colour images of 32 × 32 pixels in 10 classes. The CNN has two blocks
of convolution and max-pooling, which learn local patterns such as edges and textures. A dense layer of 256 neurons
and a softmax output then turn those patterns into a probability for each class. Pixels are scaled to 0–1, labels are
one-hot encoded, 10,000 training images are held back for validation, and early stopping halts training when the
validation loss stops improving.


Training. Early stopping halted training after 5 epochs. Training accuracy kept rising (45 % → 72 %), but
validation accuracy levelled off at about 64 %, so the model was starting to overfit. Test accuracy was 64.6 %,
against 10 % for random guessing and 67.0 % in the author's original run.


Changing the test image (the activity's question). For test images 1 to 16, 13 were predicted correctly,
including the original example (image 16, dog, 54 % confidence). The three mistakes were:


    

  • image 4, a frog predicted as a deer with 83 % confidence: a confident mistake;
    • 

  • image 10, an airplane predicted as a deer (46 %);
    • 

  • image 12, a dog predicted as a deer (49 %).
    • 



Many correct predictions were also uncertain: several ships and airplanes were classified with only 41–55 %
confidence.


Which classes are hard? Accuracy ranges from 86 % for automobiles (then frog 80 %, horse 75 %) down to
cat 42 %, dog 46 % and bird 51 %. The most common confusions are between similar-looking classes:
dog → cat (188 images), truck → automobile (172) and bird → deer (135). At 32 × 32 pixels, a cat and a dog
look much alike.


Confidence is not the same as correctness. Correct predictions averaged 78.8 % confidence and wrong ones 57.0 %.
However, 256 mistakes (7.2 % of all errors) were made with over 90 % confidence, so a high score is not proof
that the answer is right.


Small, harmless changes alter individual decisions.

Overall accuracy hardly moves, but almost a third of individual predictions change when a picture is simply
mirrored. A result that looks stable in aggregate can still be unreliable for the individual case. That matters most
when each prediction concerns a person, as in facial recognition.


Reproducibility. The seeds are fixed, but running the notebook twice gave different results (63.3 % and then
64.6 % test accuracy, with different images misclassified), because multi-threaded training on a CPU is not exactly
repeatable. Results should be reported with this variation in mind, not as a single exact number.


Link to the ethics reading¶
Wall (2019) asks how far we should trust computer vision when its decisions affect people. This small experiment shows
the same weaknesses on a harmless task:


    

  • accuracy varies widely between classes;
    • 

  • the model makes confident mistakes;
    • 

  • predictions are fragile to small changes in the image;
    • 

  • the results depend on the run.
    • 



The separate reflection draft (9.Unit09 Ethics reflection draft - Wall 2019.txt) discusses what this means for
facial recognition.
